These repeated retries are the clearest evidence of failure. The first press attempt looks close but insufficient. The analysis reports that the active left end-effector gets as close as 0.018 m to the press target at step 106. But “near the press target” is not the same as actually pushing the button inward by the required 0.02 m along the button normal. The task is strict: sideways contact or contact on the pillar face beside the button produces no motion. So the fact that the hand target is approximately reached does not prove success; the repeated retries strongly imply the contact geometry was off enough that the button did not actuate.

The first full press-retract sequence ends with the robot in phase 3 at step 101 and still in retract at step 106. During this interval the base remains stopped, the left hand stays extended near the surface, and the pelvis is somewhat lowered. Yet after the retract timeout, the controller returns to approach at step 131 because its own “ready_to_press” condition is no longer satisfied. This indicates the body drifted or overshot slightly during or after the press. The second attempt takes much longer in align phase. The phase transition 1->2 does not occur until step 216, far later than in the first attempt. The more subtle issue is the manipulation geometry. The press target in the pelvis frame for the active hand has x in [0.271, 0.450], y in [0.080, 0.340], z in [0.191, 0.200]. The likely failure mode, supported by the rollout data, is that the controller’s stand location and press target leave too little margin for robust normal-direction contact. The stand point is offset 0.45 m outward from the button face center, while the robot’s arm reach from the pelvis is limited and the press target x is frequently clamped near maximum reach. The analysis explicitly shows press target x can hit 0.450, the action limit. When the target is at or near this limit, small body-position or orientation errors translate into significant contact errors at the hand. That is compatible with the policy repeatedly getting visually close without definitively pressing the button.

There is also evidence that the success conditions for entering press are too permissive relative to actual contact success. The policy first believes it is ready to press at 0.90 s, but the minimum stand-point distance over the whole episode is not reached until much later at 6.92 s. Similarly, the first best lateral alignment occurs extremely early at step 48, yet the base later continues to reposition and retry. This gap between internal readiness metrics and actual physical success suggests the controller transitions into pressing before the combined base-arm configuration is truly robust.

So overall, the robot does many parts of the task correctly: it chooses a sensible arm, approaches the correct side, orients well, and repeatedly brings the hand near the intended contact region. It fails because “near” is not enough for this button task. The contact must be inward along the face normal, and the policy’s geometry appears too tight: it stops and presses from a stance that is only marginally reachable, often with the commanded press target near the arm’s forward limit, causing repeated almost-correct contacts and multiple retries instead of a decisive button push.

<summary>
The policy’s intended strategy is straightforward: pick the arm corresponding to the button side, walk to a standing point offset in front of the button face, face into the pillar, move the active hand to a pre-press pose, then push inward and retract.

In this rollout, that high-level plan mostly worked at the navigation level. The robot consistently used the left arm, approached the correct side of the pillar, reduced stand-point distance from 0.80 m to as low as 0.021 m, and achieved near-perfect yaw alignment. It entered the align and press phases multiple times, and the left hand came very close to the commanded press target, with minimum actual EE-to-target error of 0.018 m. Visually, the hand repeatedly reached the button area.

But the task was not completed robustly. The controller cycled through approach/align/press/retract three times, ending still in press phase. That means it got close repeatedly without producing a decisive button actuation.

The root cause is that the press geometry is too marginal. The policy declares “ready” too early and commands a press from a stance that is only barely reachable, often with the hand target near the forward action limit. Small pose errors then turn into contact errors, so the hand reaches near the button but not with reliable inward normal push.
</summary>
